title: UniSuper bond losses deepen as inflation persists
full_text:
UniSuper’s bond option has fallen 1.5 per cent in the opening quarter of the 2027 financial year, with chief investment officer John Pearce warning that persistent inflation and rising yields continue to challenge fixed income investments.
The quarterly decline followed a return of 1.2 per cent over the previous financial year, when the bond option was the fund’s worst performer.
In an investment update, Pearce said the relentless rise in yields since the pandemic had continued, with the speed of the increase adding to the pressure on markets.
Australian 10-year bond yields had climbed from about 1 to 1.2 per cent in 2022 to closer to 5.5 per cent, he said, describing the move as both a return to more normal conditions and a reflection of ongoing inflation.
UniSuper was also building its cash holdings by retaining inflows, with Pearce anticipating greater volatility as the inflation outlook remained uncertain.
“Having said that, we are building on our cash levels at the moment. We’re not selling, we’re not outright selling, but we are banking the inflows,” Pearce said.
“We believe there is going to be more volatility, particularly with the uncertain outlook for inflation.”
His assessment of inflation highlighted pressures on both supply and demand, including the effects of the pandemic, wars in Iran and Ukraine, tariffs, government spending and the investment cycle in artificial intelligence.
While Pearce hoped supply disruptions would ease, he was less confident that demand pressures would abate, pointing to continuing government budget deficits and AI expenditure.
“I’m not so hopeful on the demand side. I don’t see any restraint shown by governments and the AI investment cycle will continue at pace.”
Pearce said these conditions left central banks with little choice but to raise interest rates, noting that the Reserve Bank’s current tightening cycle remained smaller than the five previous cycles since it began targeting inflation in the 1990s.
Despite the difficult quarter for bonds, his broader investment outlook remained reasonably positive, with higher yields offering investors opportunities to earn returns without taking substantial risk.
He also believed earnings growth could support share markets, even as higher interest rates created a more challenging backdrop.
“So, no, I don’t believe the share market has become disconnected from the bond market. In fact, despite the fact that the S&P 500 is trading close to its all-time highs, I reckon it’s pretty fairly priced.”
That confidence in the broader market did not extend to every investment opportunity, with Pearce explaining why UniSuper would not participate meaningfully in the proposed Firmus initial public offering, which has since been shelved.
At the time of recording, the AI cloud services company was seeking to raise about $7 billion at a total market valuation of around $44 billion.
“We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn’t have a compelling valuation. At the current valuation, it’s priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation.”
Pearce said UniSuper could nevertheless hold Firmus shares through its index strategies or external managers, while raising concerns about the company’s need for further debt and equity to fund expansion.
A note accompanying the update said reports emerging between recording and release indicated the IPO could be shelved unless materially repriced.
